When something is objective, it is based entirely on facts and reality — not on personal feelings, personal opinions, or personal biases. An objective view of something is one that would remain the same no matter who is looking at it, because it is anchored to what is actually, verifiably true.

Think of it this way: imagine a thermometer reads 38°C. That is an objective fact. It does not matter if you love hot weather or hate it, if you are in a good mood or a bad one — the thermometer says 38°C, and that is that. No one's feelings can change that number.
Objective vs. Subjective — The Essential Contrast

The best way to truly understand "objective" is to place it next to its opposite: subjective.

Something subjective is shaped by a person's inner world — their feelings, their personal taste, their background, their mood, their interests. It varies from person to person because it lives inside the individual.

Something objective is shaped by the external world — by facts, evidence, and reality. It does not vary based on who the person is, because it exists outside any individual.

Here is a simple side-by-side to feel the difference:

"That painting is beautiful." — This is subjective. Beauty is a feeling. Someone else might find the same painting ugly, and neither person is wrong — they simply feel differently.

"That painting is 200 years old." — This is objective. Either it was made 200 years ago or it wasn't. It is a fact you can verify, and no one's personal feelings can change it.
When We Use It to Describe a Person

When you call a person objective, you mean they are being fair, neutral, and unbiased. They are not letting their personal likes, dislikes, relationships, or emotions cloud their judgment. They are looking at the situation as it truly is, rather than as they wish it to be or fear it to be.

For example: "We need an objective judge for this competition — someone who doesn't know any of the participants personally." Here, "objective" means the judge will assess the competitors purely on their performance, not on who they like or dislike.

This is why "objective" carries a positive, trustworthy quality when used about a person. An objective person is seen as reliable, honest, and fair, because their conclusions come from reality rather than from personal interest.
When We Use It to Describe an Opinion, Analysis, or Assessment

You will very often see "objective" attached to words like opinion, view, analysis, assessment, or judgment. In all these cases, the meaning is the same: the opinion or analysis is grounded in facts and evidence, not in personal feeling.

"Please give me your objective opinion on my business plan." — Here, the speaker is asking you to set aside whether you like them personally, whether you want to make them feel good, or whether you have a personal stake in the matter. They want you to look at the facts of the plan and give an honest, uncolored assessment.

"An objective analysis of the data shows that sales have declined." — Here, "objective" signals that the analysis is not being twisted to look better or worse than it actually is. It reflects what the data genuinely shows.
When We Use It to Describe Reality or Truth

"Objective" is also used to describe things that exist in the real world independently of what any person thinks or feels about them. This is especially common in philosophy and science, but you will encounter it in everyday conversation too.

"Objective reality" means the world as it actually is, separate from how any individual perceives it. The Earth orbiting the Sun is an objective reality — it was true before humans knew about it, and it would remain true even if every human believed otherwise.

"Objective truth" similarly means a fact that holds regardless of personal perspective, culture, or belief.
The Honest Complexity: Can Anything Be Perfectly Objective?

Here is something important to understand, especially when you encounter this word in real conversations: pure, complete objectivity is very hard for human beings to fully achieve. Every person carries some degree of bias, preference, and background that subtly shapes how they see the world.

So when people say someone is being "objective," they usually mean that person is trying their best to be fair and fact-based — they are making a strong effort to remove personal bias from their thinking. It is more of a quality on a spectrum than a perfect, absolute state. The more a view is grounded in evidence and the less it is colored by personal feeling, the more objective it is.

This also means that calling someone objective is a form of praise — it signals that you trust their judgment because they are not distorting reality for personal reasons.
A Quick Feel for the Word in Action

"She gave an objective review of the restaurant — she praised the good food but honestly pointed out the slow service, even though the chef is her friend."

"Try to be objective when evaluating your own work. Ask yourself what a stranger would honestly think of it."

"The court needs objective evidence — eyewitness feelings are not enough; we need facts."

"It is hard to be objective about your own children. Most parents think their child is exceptional."

Objective means: based on facts and reality, not on personal feelings, bias, or opinion. When a person, view, or analysis is objective, it reflects the world as it actually is — not as someone wishes, fears, or imagines it to be.
